What "makes" someone an intellectual coward in what way?

What defines one? Or what leads a person to become one?

I'll take a stab at both.

An intellectual coward is a person who's afraid to fully consider his own viewpoints, and thus afraid to fully consider other viewpoints, since that would necessarily lead to fully considering his own. He uses fallacies and empty and emotive rhetoric to divert from an actual consideration of the topic at hand so that he can continue to cling to his own preconceptions and continue to avoid honestly considering them.

As near as I can tell, people become intellectual cowards primarily because they have an emotional investment in their preconceptions. Generally it's that they've based some portion of their self-image on their identification with a particular view, so to question that would be to question their own self-image. That's a scary thing to many people, since undermining some aspect of their self-image would leave a "gap" that they'd then have to fill.

Years ago, in an otherwise mediocre book called The Crack in the Cosmic Egg, I read a visual analogy of this process that's stuck with me ever since.

Visualize it like this: each individual has a central core of "self" - consciousness that lives inside their minds. Think of that as the yolk of an egg.

Each individual surrounds that yolk with representations of "self" that they display to the world - attitudes, beliefs, norms and the like. Think of those as coming together to make up the shell around the fragile yolk of their egg. It's the hard surface that they expose to the world, and it's intended in large part to protect the fragile core inside of them.

All the little individual bits and pieces that are combined to form that shell are gathered together over many years. Some of them are strong and durable pieces, but others of them are not. Some of them fit well with each other, but others of them don't. Some of them are removed over time and replaced with others, but some of them - even ones that are weak or really don't fit well - are left in place.

Often, a person will end up with a piece of their shell, or even a considerable section of it, that's unstable. It might be unstable because it's founded on a misconception of reality or it might be unstable just because it doesn't fit well with the rest of their shell. In any event, all too often, instead of removing and replacing those pieces with things that fit better, they try to leave them in place. That's the root of intellectual cowardice, right there. They're afraid to remove those pieces, and instead set about trying to work out a way to justify leaving them there, or to at least avoid having to face the prospect of removing and replacing them.

Since the pieces are unstable, leaving them there requires propping them up and/or protecting them. There are any number of ways that people do that. They might put patches around the unstable parts to try to keep them in place, or they might put a wall up to keep others from poking at them. Often they'll put guns on top of the wall, in order to actually drive people away from those unstable parts of their shell. Whatever it takes, really, just so long as they can leave those parts in place and hopefully at least minimize the risk that they'll come tumbling down. And the more they feel those parts are under threat, and the more they continue to refuse to consider removing and replacing them, the more desperate their protective measures have to become. That's the real growth of intellectual cowardice - when it becomes a way of life rather than just a temporary and ill-considered protective measure.

And it's all a vicious circle. The more they invest in protecting and propping up those unstable sections of their shell, the further they get from the possibility of removing and replacing them, and the more desperately they have to try to protect them and prop them up. And, ironically, their shells just continue to grow less stable the more desperately they try to protect them - the more crap they have surrounding them and hanging off of them and wedged into the ever-growing cracks.

And so on... that should be more than enough to get the concept.

Back to intellectual cowardice: what are the effects? Primarily, the effect of intellectual cowardice is to keep alive irrational ideas that should've been set aside long ago. A close secondary effect is to keep in positions of influence people who self-evidently don't warrant it - people whose own intellectual cowardice has led them to create particularly notable webs of lies and diversions that others who share their particular intellectual cowardice find helpful in their own attempts to prop up and protect their unstable eggs. And the overall effect has certainly been to act as a drag on humanity - to slow and even prevent the advances that could've happened at the urging of intellectual pioneers in order to protect the cowards from the perceived threat of restructuring their own thinking.

And the hell of it is that removing unstable parts from ones egg and replacing them with more stable parts is almost effortless once one gets the hang of it. It's really just as easy as could be - all it takes is a bit of honesty and a bit of courage. And it gets easier every time you do it, since you'll find yourself growing ever more content and confident, as more of the unstable parts of your egg are removed and as it then grows ever stronger and more stable. Soon you'll be eagerly and proudly swapping out weak and unstable parts of your egg for stronger and more stable parts, and reveling in the confidence the ever more stable egg gives you, and you'll understand that there was never anything to be afraid of, and only wish you'd started doing it years ago.
